read.sections.0.heading.back: A town on a river bank

read.sections.0.text.note: "Viet Nam" is written "Vietnam", the usual Indonesian spelling.
read.sections.0.text.back: Hội An is a town in central Vietnam, near the place where the Thu Bồn River meets the sea. From the 1400s to the 1800s, this town was a busy trading port. Boats brought goods by water, and people on land sold, loaded and carried those goods. The river and the sea connected this town with traders from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. But not everyone in Hội An was a trader who came to visit. Local residents also built their lives there. This town's location helps explain why a port grew there. Its location cannot tell us who held power, or how each family lived.
read.sections.0.text.source: Hội An is a town in central Viet Nam, near the place where the Thu Bồn River meets the sea. From the 1400s to the 1800s, it was a busy trading port. Boats brought goods by water, and people on land sold, loaded and carried them. The river and the sea connected the town with traders from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. But not everyone in Hội An was a visiting trader. Local people built their lives there too. The town's location helps explain why a port grew there. It cannot tell us who had power, or how each family lived.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: Hội An is a town in Vietnam. This town is near a river and the sea. For about 400 years, this town was a busy port. Boats came bringing goods. People on land sold and carried those goods. Traders came from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. Local residents also lived there. The river helps us see why a port grew here. The river does not tell us how each family lived.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: Hội An is a town in Viet Nam. It is near a river and the sea. For about 400 years, it was a busy port. Boats came with goods. People on land sold and carried the goods. Traders came from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. Local people lived there too. The river helps us see why a port grew here. It does not tell us how each family lived.

read.sections.1.text.back: In 1999, UNESCO, a part of the United Nations, put Hội An on the list of World Heritage sites. Its description says that the old town has shops, homes, an open market and a ferry quay. Many buildings face the street, so buyers could come in. Their back part opens to the river, so goods could be put onto boats or taken off boats. From this, we can make an inference: the river and the street were both important for trade. UNESCO says that its buildings mix local ways with ideas mostly from China and Japan, and then later from Europe. This is a modern account, not the diary of a trader from the 1500s.
read.sections.1.text.source: In 1999, UNESCO, a part of the United Nations, listed Hội An as a World Heritage site. Its description says the old town has shops, homes, an open market and a ferry quay. Many buildings face the street, so customers could walk in. Their backs open to the river, so goods could go on and off boats. From this, we can make an inference: the river and the street were both important for trade. UNESCO says the buildings mix local ways with mostly Chinese and Japanese ideas, and later European ones. This is a modern account, not a diary from a trader in the 1500s.

The river and the street both helped trade. UNESCO wrote this in modern times. This is not a diary from the past.

read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a photo of a covered bridge in Hội An, taken in 2018. That bridge is part of that town's heritage, a place people value and look after until now. That photo shows what that bridge looked like on that day. That photo cannot show the first traders who used that port centuries ago, or what each of its residents thought. A map helps us see connections that may have existed, and a photo lets us look at a place now. To hear the view of a resident from the past, we need other sources, such as old records or old objects.
read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a photo of a covered bridge in Hội An, taken in 2018. The bridge is part of the town's heritage, a place people value and look after today. The map helps us see possible connections, and the photo lets us look at a place now. To hear a resident's view from long ago, we would need other sources, such as old records or objects.

watch.summary.back: This is a short film a few minutes long. NHK, a broadcasting station from Japan, made it together with UNESCO. This film is part of a series of films about World Heritage sites. UNESCO's record about this film says that this film is about that old town and its covered bridge, often called the Japanese Bridge. That record describes Hội An in a few words. Hội An is an old trading port that has been well looked after. That town was a port from the 1400s to the 1800s. Its buildings and street layout show a mix of local ways and ideas from other places. Remember that a camera records a place on one day. This film shows Hội An in modern times, not the busy port of the past.

educatorNotes.0.back: Aim: learners explain one way that port connected people, with a detail from a source, and name one resident's view that an account centred on buildings does not include. Step for reading evidence: trace the idea of loading goods from street to river in UNESCO's description (buildings face the street, their back part opens to the river), then point to the photo's date, 2018, before learners say what that photo shows. A good answer gives one connection supported by evidence and one source about residents that is not yet there.
educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners explain one way the port connected people, using a source detail, and name one resident's view a building-centred account leaves out. Evidence move: trace the street-to-river loading idea in UNESCO's description (buildings face the street, backs open to the river), then point to the photo's date, 2018, before learners say what it shows. educatorNotes.1.back: Misunderstanding to straighten out: that a photo taken later is a picture of the port's daily life in an earlier time. Also, "Chinese and Japanese influences" on buildings do not tell us every resident's ancestry, and local residents were not passive; the bridge's popular name does not tell us who built or used it. UNESCO's listing dates that wooden bridge, with a pagoda on it, to the 18th century, while other accounts say there was an earlier first bridge, so this lesson does not give that bridge a date. Notes on the sources: UNESCO's account is a modern interpretation of buildings that still survive; that photo shows a lower modern bridge in front of it and many visitors in 2018. For an extra comparison with another port that records local residents' voices, see George Town World Heritage Incorporated's oral history work, but do not make it a second example.
educatorNotes.1.source: Misconception to address: that a later photo is a picture of the port's earlier daily life. Also, "Chinese and Japanese influences" in buildings do not tell us every resident's ancestry, and local people were not passive; the bridge's popular name does not tell us who built or used it. UNESCO's listing dates the wooden bridge, with a pagoda on it, to the 18th century, while other accounts give an earlier first bridge, so the lesson does not date it. Source caveats: UNESCO's account is a modern interpretation of surviving buildings; the photo shows a lower modern footbridge in front and crowds of visitors in 2018. For an optional comparison with another port that records local voices, see George Town World Heritage Incorporated's oral history work, but do not make it a second case.
